quiz.0.question: At which point does weather most critically affect Barolo vintage quality?
quiz.0.options.1: Late summer ripening (August–September) and harvest timing
quiz.0.explanation: Nebbiolo ripens very late (often October). The critical window is late August through harvest — heat accumulation, rain during harvest and temperature swings during final maturation determine the vintage's character.
quiz.1.question: What is the main stylistic difference between the great 2016 and 2013 vintages?
quiz.1.options.1: 2016 is more classical, elegant and age-worthy; 2013 is richer, opulent and approachable earlier
quiz.1.options.3: 2016 was affected by hail and is uneven
quiz.1.explanation: 2016 is the more 'classic' Barolo — perfect Nebbiolo structure with razor-sharp acidity and iron tannins built for 30+ years. 2013 is equally superb but riper and more immediately seductive.
quiz.2.question: In a difficult vintage, which Barolo village should you prioritise?
quiz.2.options.1: Castiglione Falletto or Serralunga (higher elevation, better drainage)
quiz.2.options.2: All villages perform equally in difficult vintages
quiz.2.explanation: In rain-challenged vintages, the well-drained, higher-elevation communes (Castiglione Falletto, Serralunga d'Alba) tend to outperform lower-lying, heavier-soil La Morra and Barolo village.
quiz.3.question: Which Barolo vintage purchasing strategy is most sensible?
quiz.3.options.0: Always buy the most recent vintage
quiz.3.options.1: Buy top vintages (2016, 2013, 2010) on release or early, then cellar for 10–20 years
quiz.3.options.3: Buy only from one village for consistency
quiz.3.explanation: The classic strategy: buy great vintages (2010, 2013, 2016, 2019) on release while they are still available at producer prices, then cellar. Great Barolo typically needs 10–15 years and can last 30–40 years.
